subproblems.title: Adapted frame of a nonzero functional ℓ on ℝ^{m+1}: norm-preserving ι : ℝ^m → ℝ^{m+1}, e ⟂ range ι with ℓ(e) = 1, and p with ι(p(u)) + ℓ(u)e = u
subproblems.statement: Let m ∈ ℕ and let ℓ : ℝ^{m+1} → ℝ be a nonzero continuous linear functional (ℝ^k = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin k) with the Euclidean inner product ⟨·,·⟩ and norm |·|). Then there are continuous linear maps ι : ℝ^m → ℝ^{m+1} and p : ℝ^{m+1} → ℝ^m and a vector e ∈ ℝ^{m+1} such that ℓ(e) = 1, |ι(v)| = |v| and ⟨ι(v), e⟩ = 0 for every v ∈ ℝ^m, and ι(p(u)) + ℓ(u)·e = u for every u ∈ ℝ^{m+1}.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (m : ℕ) (ℓ : Eucl (m + 1) →L[ℝ] ℝ), ℓ ≠ 0 → ∃ (ι : Eucl m →L[ℝ] Eucl (m + 1)) (p : Eucl (m + 1) →L[ℝ] Eucl m) (e : Eucl (m + 1)), ℓ e = 1 ∧ (∀ v, ‖ι v‖ = ‖v‖) ∧ (∀ v, inner ℝ (ι v) e = 0) ∧ ∀ u, ι (p u) + ℓ u • e = u
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Step 1 of the parent proof (slicing_im_st_level_set_charts): "Let a ∈ ℝ^{m+1} be the gradient of ℓ := Dh(w₀) (ℓ(u) = ⟨a, u⟩, a ≠ 0) and e := a/|a|², so ℓ(e) = 1. The kernel K₀ := ker ℓ = a^⊥ has dimension m. Fix a linear isometry ι₀ : ℝ^m → ℝ^{m+1} with range K₀ (from an orthonormal basis of K₀ indexed by Fin m; ι₀ = 0 if m = 0)", together with the inverse of the linear isomorphism (v, s) ↦ ι₀v + se of Step 4. Here ℓ is an arbitrary nonzero functional and the frame is packaged as (ι, p, e).

Conventions. ℝ^k = Eucl k = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin k) with inner product ⟨·,·⟩ (inner ℝ) and Euclidean norm |·|; B(x, r) = ball x r is the open ball; Df(x) := fderiv ℝ f x for a map f.

1. (Gradient vector.) ℝ^{m+1} is a finite-dimensional, hence complete, real inner product space, so by the Riesz representation theorem there is a ∈ ℝ^{m+1} with ℓ(u) = ⟨a, u⟩ for all u (Lean: a := (InnerProductSpace.toDual ℝ (Eucl (m+1))).symm ℓ and InnerProductSpace.toDual_symm_apply). If a = 0 then ℓ(u) = 0 for all u, i.e. ℓ = 0, contrary to the hypothesis; so a ≠ 0 and |a| ≠ 0.

2. (The vector e.) Put e := |a|⁻²·a. Then ℓ(e) = |a|⁻²⟨a, a⟩ = |a|⁻²|a|² = 1 (inner_smul_right, real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq).

3. (dim ker ℓ = m.) Since ℓ ≠ 0 there is u₀ with ℓ(u₀) ≠ 0 (otherwise ℓ = 0 by extensionality). Every y ∈ ℝ equals ℓ((y/ℓ(u₀))·u₀), so range ℓ = ℝ, which has dimension 1. By rank–nullity (LinearMap.finrank_range_add_finrank_ker), 1 + dim ker ℓ = dim ℝ^{m+1} = m + 1 (finrank_euclideanSpace_fin), hence K := ker ℓ has dimension m.

4. (An isometry from ℝ^m onto K.) K is a finite-dimensional inner product space (with the restricted inner product) of dimension m. Take an orthonormal basis of K and index it by Fin m (stdOrthonormalBasis ℝ K, reindexed along finCongr : Fin (finrank ℝ K) ≃ Fin m). Its coordinate map is a linear isometric equivalence K ≃ ℝ^m (OrthonormalBasis.repr); let J : ℝ^m ≃ K be its inverse, again a linear isometric equivalence. Define the continuous linear map ι := (inclusion K ↪ ℝ^{m+1}) ∘ J. The norm of K is the restriction of the norm of ℝ^{m+1}, so |ι(v)| = |J(v)| = |v| for every v ∈ ℝ^m. (If m = 0 then K = {0} and ι = 0.)

5. (Orthogonality to e.) For v ∈ ℝ^m we have ι(v) = J(v) ∈ K = ker ℓ, so 0 = ℓ(ι(v)) = ⟨a, ι(v)⟩. Hence ⟨ι(v), e⟩ = |a|⁻²⟨ι(v), a⟩ = |a|⁻²⟨a, ι(v)⟩ = 0 (symmetry of the real inner product).

6. (The left inverse p.) For u ∈ ℝ^{m+1}, ℓ(u − ℓ(u)e) = ℓ(u) − ℓ(u)ℓ(e) = 0 by step 2, so the continuous linear map u ↦ u − ℓ(u)e (that is, id − ℓ.smulRight e) takes values in K. Let q : ℝ^{m+1} → K be its corestriction to K (ContinuousLinearMap.codRestrict), and put p := J⁻¹ ∘ q, a continuous linear map ℝ^{m+1} → ℝ^m. Then ι(p(u)) = J(J⁻¹(q(u))) = q(u) = u − ℓ(u)e (LinearIsometryEquiv.apply_symm_apply), i.e. ι(p(u)) + ℓ(u)e = u for every u.

7. (Conclusion.) ι, p and e satisfy ℓ(e) = 1 (step 2), |ι(v)| = |v| (step 4), ⟨ι(v), e⟩ = 0 (step 5) and ι(p(u)) + ℓ(u)e = u (step 6). ∎

Remark (not needed for the statement). Since ℓ(ι(v)) = 0 and p(ι(v) + se) = J⁻¹(ι(v)) = v, the maps (v, s) ↦ ι(v) + se and u ↦ (p(u), ℓ(u)) are mutually inverse linear isomorphisms ℝ^m × ℝ ≅ ℝ^{m+1}; this is the linear isomorphism of Step 4 of the parent proof.

subproblems.title: A real function that is C¹ at a point agrees on a ball around it with a globally C¹ function
subproblems.statement: Let m ∈ ℕ, g : ℝ^m → ℝ and x ∈ ℝ^m (ℝ^m = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m)), and assume g is of class C¹ at x (ContDiffAt ℝ 1 g x). Then there are ρ > 0 and a function g̃ : ℝ^m → ℝ of class C¹ on all of ℝ^m (ContDiff ℝ 1 g̃) such that g̃(v) = g(v) for every v in the open ball B(x, ρ).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (m : ℕ) (g : Eucl m → ℝ) (x : Eucl m), ContDiffAt ℝ 1 g x → ∃ ρ : ℝ, 0 < ρ ∧ ∃ g' : Eucl m → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ 1 g' ∧ ∀ v ∈ ball x ρ, g' v = g v
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Steps 1–2 of the parent proof (slicing_im_st_level_set_charts): "Since g is C¹ at 0 it is C¹ on a neighbourhood of 0 (ContDiffAt.eventually); choose r₀ > 0 such that g is C¹ on B(0, 3r₀). Let χ : ℝ^m → [0, 1] be a C^∞ bump function with χ = 1 on B(0, r₀) and support in B(0, 2r₀) (ContDiffBump). Put g̃ := χ·g. Then g̃ is C¹ on ℝ^m: it is C¹ on B(0, 3r₀) as a product of C¹ functions, and it vanishes identically on the open set {|v| > 2r₀}; these two open sets cover ℝ^m. Moreover g̃ = g on B(0, r₀)." Here it is stated for an arbitrary centre x (the parent uses x = 0) and the new function is called g' in Lean.

Conventions. ℝ^k = Eucl k = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin k) with inner product ⟨·,·⟩ (inner ℝ) and Euclidean norm |·|; B(x, r) = ball x r is the open ball; Df(x) := fderiv ℝ f x for a map f.

1. (g is C¹ near x.) g is C¹ at x and 1 ≠ ∞, so g is C¹ at every point of some neighbourhood of x (ContDiffAt.eventually). Choose ε > 0 such that g is C¹ at every y ∈ B(x, ε) (Metric.mem_nhds_iff), and put ρ := ε/3 > 0; thus ε = 3ρ.

2. (Bump function.) ℝ^m is a finite-dimensional inner product space, so smooth bump functions exist on it (hasContDiffBump_of_innerProductSpace). Let χ be the bump function centred at x with inner radius ρ and outer radius 2ρ (ContDiffBump x with rIn := ρ, rOut := 2ρ; valid since 0 < ρ < 2ρ). Then χ : ℝ^m → ℝ is C^∞, in particular C¹ at every point (ContDiffBump.contDiffAt); χ(y) = 1 for every y with |y − x| ≤ ρ (ContDiffBump.one_of_mem_closedBall); and χ(y) = 0 for every y with |y − x| ≥ 2ρ (ContDiffBump.zero_of_le_dist).

3. (Definition.) Put g̃(y) := χ(y)·g(y) for y ∈ ℝ^m, and take this ρ.

4. (g̃ is C¹ on ℝ^m.) By contDiff_iff_contDiffAt it suffices to show that g̃ is C¹ at every y ∈ ℝ^m.
   - Case |y − x| < ε. Then y ∈ B(x, ε), so g is C¹ at y by step 1, and χ is C¹ at y by step 2; hence the product g̃ = χ·g is C¹ at y (ContDiffAt.mul).
   - Case |y − x| ≥ ε. Then |y − x| ≥ 3ρ > 2ρ. The set O := {z : |z − x| > 2ρ} is open, as the strict superlevel set of the continuous function z ↦ dist(z, x) (isOpen_lt), and y ∈ O. subproblems.title: Implicit-function chart at a regular point: the level set of a C¹ function near w₀ is the image of a C¹ 1-antilipschitz map ℝ^m → ℝ^{m+1}
subproblems.statement: Let m ∈ ℕ, h : ℝ^{m+1} → ℝ of class C¹, U ⊆ ℝ^{m+1} open and w₀ ∈ U with Dh(w₀) ≠ 0 (ℝ^k = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin k), Dh(w) = fderiv ℝ h w, B(0, r) the open ball in ℝ^m). Then there are a C¹ map ψ : ℝ^m → ℝ^{m+1}, a radius r > 0 and an open set W ⊆ ℝ^{m+1} with w₀ ∈ W such that: (i) |v − v′| ≤ |ψ(v) − ψ(v′)| for all v, v′ ∈ ℝ^m; (ii) for every v ∈ B(0, r): ψ(v) ∈ U, h(ψ(v)) = h(w₀) and Dh(ψ(v)) ≠ 0; (iii) for every w ∈ W with h(w) = h(w₀) there is v ∈ B(0, r) with ψ(v) = w.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (m : ℕ) (h : Eucl (m + 1) → ℝ) (U : Set (Eucl (m + 1))) (w₀ : Eucl (m + 1)), ContDiff ℝ 1 h → IsOpen U → w₀ ∈ U → fderiv ℝ h w₀ ≠ 0 → ∃ (ψ : Eucl m → Eucl (m + 1)) (r : ℝ) (W : Set (Eucl (m + 1))), ContDiff ℝ 1 ψ ∧ 0 < r ∧ IsOpen W ∧ w₀ ∈ W ∧ (∀ v v' : Eucl m, ‖v - v'‖ ≤ ‖ψ v - ψ v'‖) ∧ (∀ v ∈ ball (0 : Eucl m) r, ψ v ∈ U ∧ h (ψ v) = h w₀ ∧ fderiv ℝ h (ψ v) ≠ 0) ∧ ∀ w ∈ W, h w = h w₀ → ∃ v ∈ ball (0 : Eucl m) r, ψ v = w
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Steps 1–5 of the parent proof (slicing_im_st_level_set_charts): local graph parametrization at a regular point w₀ by the implicit function theorem for H(v, s) = h(w₀ + ι₀v + se), globalization of the implicit function g by a bump function, the Pythagorean lower bound, the choice of the chart domain, and the identification of the level set inside W with ψ(V). The open set U plays the role of Ω, and the frame (ι₀, e) together with the inverse of (v, s) ↦ ι₀v + se is supplied by the sibling kernel_frame; the bump-function globalization is the sibling c1_extension.

Conventions. ℝ^k = Eucl k = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin k) with inner product ⟨·,·⟩ (inner ℝ) and Euclidean norm |·|; B(x, r) = ball x r is the open ball; Df(x) := fderiv ℝ f x for a map f. On ℝ^m × ℝ we use the product (max) norm, so the ball of radius ε about (0, 0) is B(0, ε) × (−ε, ε) (ball_prod_same).

1. (Frame.) Put ℓ := Dh(w₀) ≠ 0. By the sibling kernel_frame (slicing_im_st_lsc_kernel_frame applied to m and ℓ) there are continuous linear maps ι : ℝ^m → ℝ^{m+1}, p : ℝ^{m+1} → ℝ^m and a vector e ∈ ℝ^{m+1} with
   (F1) ℓ(e) = 1; (F2) |ι(v)| = |v| for all v; (F3) ⟨ι(v), e⟩ = 0 for all v; (F4) ι(p(u)) + ℓ(u)e = u for all u.

2. (The implicit equation.) Let L : ℝ^m × ℝ → ℝ^{m+1} be the continuous linear map L(v, s) := ι(v) + s·e (ι ∘ fst + snd.smulRight e), let A(q) := w₀ + L(q), so A(v, s) = w₀ + ι(v) + s·e, and let H := h ∘ A : ℝ^m × ℝ → ℝ.
   - A is affine with derivative L at every point, and A(0, 0) = w₀.
   - H is C¹ as the composition of the C¹ map h with the C¹ (affine) map A, and H(0, 0) = h(w₀).
   - By the chain rule DH(0, 0) = Dh(A(0, 0)) ∘ L = ℓ ∘ L. Its restriction to the second factor, DH(0, 0) ∘ inr : ℝ → ℝ, is s ↦ ℓ(L(0, s)) = ℓ(ι(0) + s·e) = s·ℓ(e) = s by (F1); it is the identity of ℝ, which is invertible (it is the continuous linear equivalence ContinuousLinearEquiv.refl ℝ ℝ).

3. (Implicit function theorem.) Apply the C¹ implicit function theorem of Mathlib (ContDiffAt.implicitFunction from Mathlib.Analysis.Calculus.ImplicitContDiff) to H, which is C¹ at u := (0, 0), with n := 1 ≠ 0 and the invertible partial derivative of step 2. It provides a function g : ℝ^m → ℝ such that
   (I1) g(0) = 0 (ContDiffAt.implicitFunction_apply_self: g(u.1) = u.2);
   (I2) g is C¹ at 0 (ContDiffAt.contDiffAt_implicitFunction);
   (I3) for all (v, s) in some neighbourhood N₀ of (0, 0): H(v, s) = H(0, 0) ⟺ g(v) = s (ContDiffAt.eventually_apply_eq_iff_implicitFunction).
   Choose ε > 0 with B((0, 0), ε) = B(0, ε) × (−ε, ε) ⊆ N₀ (Metric.mem_nhds_iff).

4. (Globalization of g and definition of ψ.) By (I2) and the sibling c1_extension (slicing_im_st_lsc_c1_extension applied to m, g and x := 0) there are ρ > 0 and a function g̃ : ℝ^m → ℝ of class C¹ on ℝ^m with g̃(v) = g(v) for all v ∈ B(0, ρ). Define ψ(v) := w₀ + ι(v) + g̃(v)·e. ψ is C¹ (a constant plus a continuous linear map plus the C¹ scalar function g̃ times the constant vector e). Since 0 ∈ B(0, ρ), g̃(0) = g(0) = 0 by (I1), so ψ(0) = w₀.

5. (Conclusion (i): ψ is 1-antilipschitz on ℝ^m.) Let v, v′ ∈ ℝ^m and put d := g̃(v) − g̃(v′). By linearity of ι, ψ(v) − ψ(v′) = ι(v − v′) + d·e, and ⟨ι(v − v′), d·e⟩ = d·⟨ι(v − v′), e⟩ = 0 by (F3). By the Pythagorean identity (norm_add_sq_real) and (F2),
   |ψ(v) − ψ(v′)|² = |ι(v − v′)|² + 2·0 + |d·e|² = |v − v′|² + |d·e|² ≥ |v − v′|².
   As |ψ(v) − ψ(v′)| ≥ 0, taking square roots gives |v − v′| ≤ |ψ(v) − ψ(v′)| (le_of_sq_le_sq).

6. (Choice of r.) Let O := U ∩ {w : Dh(w) ≠ 0}. Since h is C¹, Dh is continuous (ContDiff.continuous_fderiv), so {w : Dh(w) ≠ 0} is open, and O is open; w₀ ∈ O because w₀ ∈ U and Dh(w₀) ≠ 0. As ψ is continuous with ψ(0) = w₀ ∈ O, we have ψ(v) ∈ O for all v in a neighbourhood of 0. As g is continuous at 0 (by (I2)) with g(0) = 0, we have |g(v)| < ε for all v in a neighbourhood of 0. Choose r₀ > 0 such that both properties hold for all v ∈ B(0, r₀), and put r := min(r₀, ρ, ε) > 0. So r ≤ r₀, r ≤ ρ and r ≤ ε.

7. (Conclusion (ii).) Let v ∈ B(0, r).
   - Since v ∈ B(0, r₀): ψ(v) ∈ U, Dh(ψ(v)) ≠ 0 and |g(v)| < ε.
   - Since |v| < r ≤ ε and |g(v)| < ε, (v, g(v)) ∈ B(0, ε) × (−ε, ε) ⊆ N₀. Trivially g(v) = g(v), so (I3) gives H(v, g(v)) = H(0, 0) = h(w₀).
   - Since |v| < r ≤ ρ, g̃(v) = g(v), hence ψ(v) = w₀ + ι(v) + g(v)·e = A(v, g(v)) and h(ψ(v)) = H(v, g(v)) = h(w₀).

8. (The open set W.) Let W := {w ∈ ℝ^{m+1} : p(w − w₀) ∈ B(0, r) and ℓ(w − w₀) ∈ (−ε, ε)}. W is the intersection of the preimages of the open balls B(0, r) ⊆ ℝ^m and B(0, ε) ⊆ ℝ under the continuous maps w ↦ p(w − w₀) and w ↦ ℓ(w − w₀); hence W is open. Since p(0) = 0, ℓ(0) = 0 and r, ε > 0, w₀ ∈ W. (By (F4), w = A(p(w − w₀), ℓ(w − w₀)) for every w, so W = A(B(0, r) × (−ε, ε)), the open neighbourhood called W in Step 4 of the parent proof; only the identity (F4) is used below.)

9. (Conclusion (iii).) Let w ∈ W with h(w) = h(w₀). Put v := p(w − w₀) ∈ B(0, r) and s := ℓ(w − w₀) ∈ (−ε, ε).
   - By (F4) applied to u := w − w₀, ι(v) + s·e = w − w₀, so A(v, s) = w₀ + ι(v) + s·e = w.
   - Since |v| < r ≤ ε, (v, s) ∈ B(0, ε) × (−ε, ε) ⊆ N₀, and H(v, s) = h(A(v, s)) = h(w) = h(w₀) = H(0, 0). By (I3), g(v) = s.
   - Since |v| < r ≤ ρ, g̃(v) = g(v) = s, so ψ(v) = w₀ + ι(v) + s·e = A(v, s) = w.
   Thus v ∈ B(0, r) and ψ(v) = w.

10. (Conclusion.) ψ is C¹ (step 4), r > 0 (step 6), W is open with w₀ ∈ W (step 8), and (i), (ii), (iii) hold by steps 5, 7 and 9. For m = 0 every step holds verbatim: ℝ⁰ = {0}, ι = 0, p = 0, ψ is the constant w₀, W = {w : |ℓ(w − w₀)| < ε}, and (iii) says that w₀ is the only point of W on the level set {h = h(w₀)}. ∎

subproblems.title: Antilipschitz on an open neighbourhood gives the derivative lower bound c|s| ≤ |DΦ(w)s|

Conventions: ℝ^P = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin P) = Eucl P with Euclidean norm ‖·‖; L := fderiv ℝ Φ w.

 - Because t > 0, ‖t•s‖ = |t|·‖s‖ = t‖s‖ (norm_smul, Real.norm_of_nonneg). So c·(t‖s‖) ≤ X, where X := ‖Φ(w + t•s) − Φ(w)‖.
 - Also ‖t⁻¹•(Φ(w + t•s) − Φ(w))‖ = t⁻¹·X, since t⁻¹ ≥ 0.

 - Hence, after simp rewrites 0 + t to t and 0•s to 0: c‖s‖ ≤ ‖t⁻¹•(γ(0 + t) − γ(0))‖ for 𝓝[>]0-eventually all t.

6. (Pass to the limit.) The filter 𝓝[>] 0 on ℝ is nontrivial. Steps 3 and 5 give an eventual lower bound for a convergent real sequence-like family, so the bound passes to the limit (ge_of_tendsto): c‖s‖ ≤ ‖L s‖. Since s was arbitrary, c‖s‖ ≤ ‖fderiv ℝ Φ w s‖ for all s. ∎

subproblems.title: Tangent range of a parametrized regular level set: range D(Φ∘ψ)(v) = DΦ(ψ(v))(ker Dh(ψ(v)))
subproblems.statement: Let P, m ∈ ℕ (ℝ^k = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin k), D = fderiv ℝ), ψ : ℝ^m → ℝ^{m+1}, Φ : ℝ^{m+1} → ℝ^P, h : ℝ^{m+1} → ℝ, V ⊆ ℝ^m open, c > 0 and v ∈ V. Assume ψ is differentiable at v, Φ and h are differentiable at ψ(v), Dh(ψ(v)) ≠ 0, c|v′ − v″| ≤ |ψ(v′) − ψ(v″)| for all v′, v″ ∈ V, and h(ψ(v′)) = h(ψ(v)) for all v′ ∈ V. Then the range of D(Φ∘ψ)(v) equals the image under DΦ(ψ(v)) of the kernel of Dh(ψ(v)): D(Φ∘ψ)(v)(ℝ^m) = DΦ(ψ(v))(ker Dh(ψ(v))).

Source: Step 7 of the parent proof (slicing_im_st_level_set_charts) together with the injectivity claim at the end of its Step 3 ("Dψ(v) is injective with |Dψ(v)u| ≥ |u|, because |Dψ(v)u| = lim_{s→0} |ψ(v + su) − ψ(v)|/|s|"), stated for a map ψ that is c-antilipschitz on an open set V on which h∘ψ is constant. In the parent it is applied with V := B(0, r), c := 1 and ψ the graph parametrization of the sibling local_graph.

Conventions. ℝ^k = Eucl k = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin k) with inner product ⟨·,·⟩ (inner ℝ) and Euclidean norm |·|; B(x, r) = ball x r is the open ball; Df(x) := fderiv ℝ f x for a map f.

1. (Dψ(v) is injective.) By the sibling fderiv_lower_bound (lpf_wtc_cat_fderiv_lower_bound applied with Q := m + 1, n := m, Φ := ψ, Ω := V, the constant c and w := v; its hypotheses hold because V is open, v ∈ V, ψ is differentiable at v and c|v′ − v″| ≤ |ψ(v′) − ψ(v″)| for all v′, v″ ∈ V), we have c|u| ≤ |Dψ(v)u| for every u ∈ ℝ^m. If Dψ(v)a = Dψ(v)b, then by linearity c|a − b| ≤ |Dψ(v)(a − b)| = |Dψ(v)a − Dψ(v)b| = 0; since c > 0 and |a − b| ≥ 0 this forces |a − b| = 0, i.e. a = b. So Dψ(v) is injective.

2. (range Dψ(v) ⊆ ker Dh(ψ(v)).) V is open and contains v, so V is a neighbourhood of v, and h(ψ(v′)) = h(ψ(v)) for all v′ ∈ V. Hence h∘ψ coincides near v with the constant function h(ψ(v)), and therefore D(h∘ψ)(v) = 0 (Filter.EventuallyEq.fderiv_eq and fderiv_const_apply). Since h is differentiable at ψ(v) and ψ is differentiable at v, the chain rule (fderiv_comp) gives D(h∘ψ)(v) = Dh(ψ(v)) ∘ Dψ(v). Thus Dh(ψ(v))(Dψ(v)u) = 0 for every u ∈ ℝ^m, i.e. range Dψ(v) ⊆ ker Dh(ψ(v)).

3. (Both subspaces have dimension m.)
   - By step 1 and LinearMap.finrank_range_of_inj, dim range Dψ(v) = dim ℝ^m = m (finrank_euclideanSpace_fin).
   - Dh(ψ(v)) ≠ 0, so there is u₀ with Dh(ψ(v))u₀ ≠ 0 (otherwise Dh(ψ(v)) = 0 by extensionality). Every y ∈ ℝ equals Dh(ψ(v))((y / Dh(ψ(v))u₀)·u₀), so range Dh(ψ(v)) = ℝ, of dimension 1. By rank–nullity (LinearMap.finrank_range_add_finrank_ker), 1 + dim ker Dh(ψ(v)) = dim ℝ^{m+1} = m + 1, hence dim ker Dh(ψ(v)) = m.

4. (range Dψ(v) = ker Dh(ψ(v)).) By steps 2 and 3, range Dψ(v) is a subspace of the finite-dimensional space ker Dh(ψ(v)) of the same dimension, so the two are equal (Submodule.eq_of_le_of_finrank_eq).

5. (Chain rule for Φ∘ψ.) Φ is differentiable at ψ(v) and ψ at v, so D(Φ∘ψ)(v) = DΦ(ψ(v)) ∘ Dψ(v) (fderiv_comp). The range of a composite of linear maps is the image of the range of the inner map under the outer map (LinearMap.range_comp): range D(Φ∘ψ)(v) = DΦ(ψ(v))(range Dψ(v)). By step 4 this equals DΦ(ψ(v))(ker Dh(ψ(v))), i.e. LinearMap.range (fderiv ℝ (Φ ∘ ψ) v) = Submodule.map (fderiv ℝ Φ (ψ v)) (LinearMap.ker (fderiv ℝ h (ψ v))). For m = 0 both sides are {0} and the same argument applies verbatim. ∎
